William Lilye (about 1468-1522) was an English scholar born at Odiham in Hampshire. Oxford took him in 1486. A pilgrimage to Jerusalem followed his arts degree. Rhodes, Rome, and Venice fed his learning on the way home. Greek exiles and famed teachers shaped him in those years.

Back in London he taught grammar on his own. Men hold him the first to teach Greek in that city. Thomas More grew close to him. In 1510 Dean Colet set him as first high master of the new St Paul's School. Plague killed him on 25 February 1522. His lasting mark is a shared book, the old Latin grammar used at Eton for ages. Two parts are surely his: verses on noun genders and on verb forms. Latin prose and verse of his own also survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-e:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Emmeram describes a Benedictine house at Regensburg, named for the city's patron saint, its famed founder. St. Emmeram lived in the mid-seventh century, and 652 stands as the likely date of the house's start.

Its roots lay in a chapel holding much-loved relics, made larger in 697 by Theodo, Duke of Bavaria, who built a new Benedictine house with Apollonius as first abbot. Charlemagne made it larger still about 800, with wide lands and many rights. When St. Boniface split Bavaria into four sees in 739, Regensburg's first bishop set his seat at St. Emmeram, later moving it to St. Stephen's beside the present church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abel-son-of-a:
Abel was the second son of Adam, and this entry weighs what his name may mean, from vanity and shortness of life to sorrow, lamentation, or shepherd. Cain, the firstborn, farmed the soil, while Abel kept flocks, so the brothers were linked by birth and by work. Abel appears in the Old Testament only in Genesis 4, and St. Augustine reads him as a type of the regenerate man, set against Cain as the natural man.

Nothing is said of Abel's descendants, so the entry supposes he left none alive at the birth of Seth. It also covers the Abelians, a North African sect named by Augustine who claimed to imitate Abel by marrying yet refusing marital relations. Legends about Cain and Abel from the Bible, the Koran, and the Talmud close the piece, with sources for readers who want the fuller tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham:
Abraham, first called Abram, is the patriarch whose story fills Genesis 11:26 to 25:18. This entry opens with a brief outline of that life before discussing him from several angles. Thare took Abram, his wife Sarai, and Lot from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran. After Thare's death Abram obeyed God's call into Chanaan, building altars at Sichem and Bethel. A famine drove him to Egypt, where fear for his life led him to pass Sarai off as his sister.

Beyond the outline, the entry treats Abraham in the Old Testament, in the New Testament, in profane history, and in legend. It weighs the meaning of his name, from lofty father to a dialect form of Abram. It also deals with the composite character of the Genesis narrative, joining older collections with a later priestly one. Readers get both the patriarch's story and the scholarship that surrounds it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam:
Adam is the first man and father of the human race, and this long entry starts with the etymology of the Hebrew adam. The word was probably first a common noun rather than a proper name. Semitic scholars diverge on its sense, and no theory fully satisfies. The root for man or mankind appears in only some Semitic tongues, as a native term only in Phoenician, Sabean, and probably Assyrian.

Genesis 2:7 links the name with ha-adamah, the ground, making man earthborn, as Latin homo is kin to humus. That ground etymology, though defended by some, is now generally abandoned. Others read the root as to be red, a sense it bears in Old Testament passages and in Arabic and Ethiopic. Beyond etymology the entry follows Adam through Genesis, the New Testament, and the legends around him, pointing readers to the Jewish Encyclopedia and Smith and Wace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adullam:
Adullam, Hebrew Adhullam and Vulgate Odollam, names both a Chanaanite city and a cave. The city stood west of Bethlehem at the foot of Juda's mountains. From Chanaanite hands it passed to Juda, was fortified by Roboam, was mentioned by the prophet Micheas, and after the exile was repeopled by Jews.

The Cave of Adullam sheltered David and his followers, as 1 Samuel 22 records. Some place it six miles southeast of Bethlehem in Wady Khareitun, but more probably it lies near the city of Adullam itself. The entry cites Clermont-Ganneau and Conder in the Palestine Exploration Fund memoirs and Muir in Hastings's Bible dictionary for readers tracing city and cave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aelfric-abbot:
Aelfric, Abbot of Eynsham, also called the Grammarian, was author of the Anglo-Saxon homilies, a translator of scripture, and a writer on many miscellaneous subjects; born about 955, he died about 1020. His identity has drawn much controversy, and Freeman's Norman Conquest wrongly identifies him with Aelfric, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Of late years nearly all scholars have accepted Lingard and Dietrich's view that Anglo-Saxon literature knows but one famous Aelfric, who rose no higher than abbot. A monk of Winchester's Old Monastery under St. Athelwold, whose life he wrote in Latin, he was sent after ordination to Cerne Abbey in Dorset, then became abbot of newly founded Eynsham near Oxford in 1005. Most prolific of preserved Anglo-Saxon writers, he is remembered above all for his Homilies, around whose Eucharistic teaching a great controversy raged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ahicam: Ahicam, a name meaning my brother has risen, served at Josias's high court and under both his two sons, shielding Jeremias from the angry populace's deadly fury. Saphan the scribe was his father; his son Godolias later governed the country under Nabuchodonosor. Scripture names him three times: 2 Kings 22:12, Jeremiah 26:24, Jeremiah 40:5.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alan-of-walsi:
Alan of Walsingham died about 1364. A celebrated architect, he first appears in 1314, a junior monk at Ely noted for skill in goldsmith's work and acquaintance with mechanics' principles. In 1331, when sub-prior, he designed and began the cathedral's St. Mary's Chapel, now Trinity Church.

December 1321 saw him elected sacristan, with sole charge of the cathedral fabric. In February 1322 the great tower fell, carrying the choir and attached portions with it. Instead of rebuilding the four piers of the Norman square tower, Alan pushed the supports a bay into each arm of the cross. So he spread the weight on eight piers instead of four and gained a magnificent central octagonal hall, domed with a lofty lantern. The result was beautiful and in every sense original. Alan almost certainly never travelled beyond his convent, knowing domed Eastern churches only by hearsay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-of-:
Alexander of Neckam, also called Necham, was an English scholar born in Hertfordshire in 1157 and dead at Kempsey in Worcestershire in 1217. He studied at the abbey school of St. Albans and then at Paris, in the school of Petit Pons. In 1180 he began teaching with success, drawing many students by his broad knowledge and his Latin style in prose and verse.

Returning to England in 1186, Neckam taught at Dunstable and then at St. Albans. He joined the Augustinians and was chosen Abbot of Cirencester in 1213. He wrote prolifically: a grammar, commentaries on Scripture and Aristotle, theological treatises, sermons, and a verse translation of Aesop's Fables. But most of his works remain in manuscript. Only two have been printed: On the Natures of Things, covering heavens, stars, air, earth, water, and life, and the poem In Praise of Divine Wisdom. He is the first European author to mention the mariner's compass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amsterdam:
Amsterdam, capital and second residential city of the Netherlands, lies in a semicircle on the Ij at the mouth of the Amstel. It is joined to the North Sea by a canal built between 1865 and 1879. Its story starts in 1204, when Gijsbrecht II, Lord of the Amstel, built a fortress here. The settlement won city rank in 1301, then grew rich on merchants from Brabant and Flanders.

By the end of the fifteenth century more than twenty monasteries stood in the city, though only the Beguinage kept its old form through the Reformation. Pilgrims crowded the Holy Room, scene of the Miracle of Amsterdam, reached by the street still called the Holy Way. After full religious liberty came in 1848 and the hierarchy returned in 1853, Amsterdam became a deanery under Haarlem with eighteen Catholic parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-frede:
Antoine-Frederic Ozanam, a French scholar born at Milan in 1813, joined learning to charity. At eighteen he defended the faith in print, then studied law in Paris, where doubt shook him until a priest teacher restored his belief. He vowed to serve the truth that had given him peace, and he kept that vow for life.

At twenty, with seven friends, he founded the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, to back faith with works of charity. His Dante thesis won his doctorate, and he rose to the Sorbonne chair in foreign literature in 1844. His books, praised for warmth and exactness, remain readable introductions to their subjects, and he spread his charity society with tireless zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assam:
Assam is a prefecture apostolic in the Calcutta church province in India, established in 1889 and staffed by the Society of the Divine Saviour. Its mother house stands at Rome, with priests resident at Shillong. Assam covers the civil province of Assam, with Bhutan and Manipur. Its native population runs to 7,000,000, while Catholics number 1,800, served by six secular and ten regular priests.

Chapels stand at Shillong, Gauhati, Bondashill, Railing, Laitkinsew, Silchar, Cherrapunji, Lamin, and elsewhere, twenty-five chapels and nineteen stations in all. The mission also runs fifteen elementary schools with 300 pupils, two orphanages under Sisters of the Divine Saviour, four charitable dispensaries, and one asylum for aged women. It also runs a small hospital at Shillong, while seventeen non-Catholic sects count 18,000 adherents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balaam:
Balaam, son of Beor of Pethor, is the seer Balak, King of Moab, hired to curse Israel. His story runs through Numbers 22 to 24, with echoes in Deuteronomy, Joshua, Nehemiah, Micah, Peter, Jude, and Revelation. His name's derivation is uncertain, though Neubauer links it to a god called Ammo or Ammi. Balak, alarmed at Israel's victories over the Amorites, sent messengers with presents to fetch him.

Men then prized a curse highly, and Balaam held special repute: whom he blessed was blessed, and whom he cursed was cursed. He first consulted the Lord and was refused leave to go, so he sent the embassy away. A second, grander embassy won leave on condition that he speak only what God commanded. Critics date his fourth prophecy no earlier than David's reign, noting later retouching of such writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balsam:
Balsam is an oily, resinous, scented substance that flows from certain plants, by itself or by cutting. The Church mixes it with olive oil to make chrism. True balsams include the costly Balm of Gilead, or Mecca, grown in Arabia, Egypt, and Syria. Copaiva balsam and those of Peru and Tolu come chiefly from South America.

Church use of balsam is very ancient, reaching back perhaps to Apostolic times. Scarcity and price have left the Latin Church content with balm alone in holy chrism. In the East, where the climate suits such plants, the Church uses thirty-six precious perfumes in the oil. The Latin Church fixes neither amount nor quality: enough to scent the oil suffices. The mingling is meant as an outward sign of the good odor of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bedlam:
Bedlam is the popular shortening of Bethlehem, Hebrew for house of bread, a London hospital founded in 1247 as a priory in Bishopsgate Street. Simon Fitz Mary founded it for the order of St Mary of Bethlehem, to serve the poor sick and homeless. By the fourteenth century it partly housed the insane, as a 1405 Royal Commission report shows. In 1375 it became a royal hospital, seized as an alleged alien priory, and later reverted to the city.

By Tyndale's day the word meant a madman, and in 1547 Henry VIII granted Bedlam with St Bartholomew's to London. A new hospital rose at Finsbury Circus in 1674, and the old site now holds Liverpool Street station. Hogarth pictured fashionable ladies visiting it as a show, and after an 1851 investigation it came under regular inspection. It now houses about three hundred patients with over sixty attendants, curing more than half each year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-birmingham:
Birmingham, an English diocese, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. One of thirteen dioceses restored by Pius IX in 1850, it covers Oxford, Stafford, Warwick, and Worcester, taking its name from Birmingham, the largest town of the four counties. Before 1850 the same counties lay in the Midland, then Central, vicariate, ruled by vicars-apostolic since 1688.

Bishop Milner, learned in controversy, was its most illustrious vicar, and William Bernard Ullathorne became its first bishop, enthroned at St. Chad's in 1850 with Newman preaching. Oscott College, home to converts, anchors its story. The entry joins restoration history to a working diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-cot:
Blessed Thomas Cottam, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Lancashire in 1549 to Protestant parents, he was executed at Tyburn in 1582. After Brasenose College, Oxford, and a London grammar-school mastership, Thomas Pound converted him, and he went to Douai, ordained deacon at Cambrai in 1577.

Hoping for the Indian mission, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Rome in 1579, but fever sent him to Lyons and then Reims, where he joined the English mission instead. Arrested on landing, he was racked and tried with Campion's companions. The entry presents a convert whose mission changed from India to England's scaffold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-josep:
An encyclopedia life of Charles Joseph Kickham, Irish patriot, novelist, and poet from County Tipperary. Born in 1828, he lost much of his sight and hearing as a boy when a flask of damp gunpowder exploded while he dried it. He joined the Young Ireland rising of 1848, then the Fenians, a secret movement for Irish independence, and helped edit their paper, The Irish People, until his arrest in 1865.

Sentenced to fourteen years of penal servitude, a harsh prison punishment, Kickham's health broke down, and he was freed in 1869 nearly blind. He then turned wholly to writing, producing novels of rural Irish life, above all Knocknagow, published in 1879 and praised as a faithful portrait of a Tipperary village. His fiction blends humour and pathos, a tender sadness, with close observation of small farmers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chatham:
A history of the Diocese of Chatham, which covers the northern half of New Brunswick in Canada. The land once belonged to the Diocese of Quebec, then to St. John, until St. John was divided on 8 May 1860 and Chatham was created. James Rogers, consecrated in August of that year, arrived to find only seven priests for a vast country, much of it French Acadian.

Rogers ruled for forty-two years and left a diocese of forty-seven parishes and fifty-one priests when he resigned in 1902. His successor, Thomas Francis Barry, and the diocese then counted fifty-seven churches with resident priests and twenty-five missions, serving about 66,000 Catholics. Its schools included a classical college at Caraquet run by the Eudist Fathers, eight parish schools, and three schools taught by sisters. Two orphan asylums and four hospitals served the diocese, among them, Tracadie's government hospital for lepers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-schra:
Dominic Schram was a Benedictine theologian and canonist born at Bamberg on 24 October 1722. He took vows at Banz in 1743 and was ordained in 1748, then taught at his monastery in turn mathematics, canon law, philosophy, and theology. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he reluctantly became prior of Michelsberg at Bamberg in 1782 and returned to Banz five years later.

His chief works are a scientific compendium of dogmatic, scholastic, and moral theology in three volumes and an Institutions of Mystical Theology in two, judged his best. An analysis of the fathers and church writers ran to eighteen volumes, and he reworked Carranza's Summa of councils up to Pius the Sixth. He died at Banz in 1797.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-strans:
Edward Stransham was an English priest and martyr born at Oxford about 1554 and put to death at Tyburn in 1586. He took his degree at Saint John's College, Oxford, in 1575 or 1576, reached Douai in 1577, and moved with the college to Reims in 1578. Illness sent him home, but he returned to Reims in 1579 and was ordained at Soissons in December 1580.

He came back to England in June 1581 with his fellow martyr Nicholas Woodfen. In 1583 he returned to Reims with twelve Oxford converts, then spent about eighteen months at Paris near death from consumption. Arrested in Bishopsgate Street in London in July 1585 while saying Mass, he was condemned at the next assizes for being a priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haymo-of-fave:
Kent Franciscan Haymo of Faversham, a famed Paris lecturer and preacher before joining the Friars Minor about 1224, became one of the order's great reformers. As custos at Paris he helped carry the chapter's questions to Gregory IX, winning the bull Quo elongati of 1230. He later lectured at Oxford, Tours, Bologna, and Padua and negotiated reunion at Constantinople in 1233.

His revision of the Roman Curia's Breviary, published in 1241, grew into the Breviary of the whole Church. As general after Elias's deposition in 1239 he cut the provinces from seventy-two and barred lay brothers from superiors' posts where priests were available. He set friars to farming so they need not beg. He died at Anagni in 1243, praised on his tomb as England's highest glory among the Minors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-nutcomb:
Henry Nutcombe Oxenham, an English poet and controversialist, born at Harrow in 1829, studied at Harrow School and Balliol College, Oxford, and served as Anglican curate at Worminghall and St. Bartholomew's, Cripplegate, where Cardinal Manning received him into the Catholic Church. He entered St. Edmund's College intending priesthood, but left after minor orders, believing Anglican orders valid and himself already a priest, and spent the rest of his life in that anomalous position.

Oxenham's ambition was reunion of the Anglican and Catholic churches, pursued in a sympathetic reply to Pusey's Eirenicon and in his Lectures on Reunion of 1872. After the Vatican Council his unwillingness to accept papal infallibility, influenced by Döllinger, made his position stranger still. Yet he never outwardly broke with Rome and died in 1888 having received the sacraments from Father Lockhart. He also translated Döllinger's First Age of Christianity and wrote Catholic Eschatology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herbert-of-bo:
Herbert of Bosham, a biographer of St. Thomas Becket, was probably of Bosham in Sussex; his birth and death dates unknown. He joined Becket's household before 1162, when the new archbishop at once gave him a post advising on duties and directing scriptural studies. He stayed close to Thomas through episcopacy and exile to the very eve of the murder in Canterbury Cathedral. He proved the king and the royal customs' keenest antagonist, ready to beard Henry II.

After the martyrdom Herbert lived mainly on the Continent, complaining of neglect, and nothing is known of him after 1189. As biographer he enjoyed advantages as eyewitness, present at the trial at Northampton. He did not write until 1184, and his reminiscences are doubted for accuracy and exaggerating his own influence. His Life is therefore less valuable than Fitzstephen's, and extremely verbose, alongside a Liber Melorum in the martyr's praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ihs-monogram:
IHS shortens the name of Jesus Christ. Christians were already shortening the Saviour's names in inscriptions by the third century, writing IH and XP for Jesus and Christus. A century later the chi-rho sigla served as more than shorthand: it worked as a symbol too.

Yet from the start, contraction was the usual method for sacred names, giving IHS and XPS, or IC and XC, for Iesous Christos. Latin writers kept these Greek contractions through the Middle Ages. In time people forgot what they meant, and misreading IHS produced the faulty spelling Jhesus. After the twelfth century the monogram spread further, as Bernard urged devotion to the Holy Name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-commendam:
In commendam is canon-law language for one way of granting a Church benefice. Commendam itself is the accusative of commenda, a Low Latin word for trust or custody, from commendare, to entrust. At first the phrase covered a stopgap grant: a benefice with no holder yet was put in someone's care for a time.

That stood against in titulum, the normal grant without conditions. Handing out benefices this way goes back to the fourth century. Ambrose, while Bishop of Milan, mentions a church he entrusted to someone until it gained its own bishop. Orléans' Third Council in 538 placed such grants under bishops' oversight, and Gregory the Great often gave churches and monasteries this way to bishops forced from their sees by barbarian invaders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-ozana:
French mathematician Jacques Ozanam was born at Bouligneux in 1640. He died at Paris on 3 April 1717. He came from a rich family that had left Judaism for Catholicism. The better known Antoine-Frédéric Ozanam sprang from the same family. Jacques began theology to please his father. But mathematics attracted him more strongly, and he mastered it without a teacher. At fifteen he produced a mathematical treatise.

After his father's death, he quit theology after four years of study. At Lyons he began giving free private lessons in mathematics. Later, when family property passed wholly to his elder brother, he reluctantly accepted fees. In 1670 he published trigonometric and logarithmic tables more accurate than those of Ulacq, Pitiscus, and Briggs. Lending money kindly to two strangers won him notice from a patron. The entry presents a self-taught mathematician of the age of Louis XIV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeroboam:
Jeroboam is the name of two kings of Israel, and this entry begins with the first, founder of the northern kingdom after the ten tribes broke away. Son of Nebat, an Ephraimite, he rose young under Solomon, overseeing forced labour for Ephraim and Manasseh on Jerusalem's Millo fortress and other works.

Seeing discontent under Solomon's extravagance, Jeroboam heard the prophet Ahijah promise him ten tribes if he stayed faithful. Impatient, he rebelled early, fled to Egypt's King Shishak, and returned after Solomon's death to lead the plea for lighter burdens. Rehoboam's harsh refusal split the kingdom, and Jeroboam took the northern crown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-adam:
John Adam was a French Jesuit preacher and a stout opponent of Calvinists and Jansenists. A native of Limoges, born in 1608, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1622 and died at Bordeaux in 1684. His writings defended the Eucharist and attacked his opponents head-on, with titles such as Calvin Defeated by Himself and The Tomb of Jansenism.

He also wrote a week-long controversy on the sacrament of the altar, an abridged life of St. Francis Borgia, Lenten sermons, books of devotion and hymn translations. His views on Saint Augustine brought him into collision with Cardinal Noris. Noris attacked him in his Vindications of Augustine. Another critic assailed the errors and invectives he was said to have uttered in a Lenten sermon at Saint Paul's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-fecke:
John de Feckenham was the last Abbot of Westminster, a Benedictine who faced Elizabeth's settlement with courage and mildness. Born in Feckenham Forest about 1515 to poor parents named Howman, he became a monk at Evesham, studied at Oxford, and taught until the dissolution in 1540. Imprisoned in the Tower under Edward VI for defending the faith, he was freed by Mary, made Dean of St. Paul's in 1554, and prepared Lady Jane Grey for death.

Appointed abbot of the restored Westminster in 1556, he led some twenty-eight monks, defended sanctuary rights in Parliament, and restored the Confessor's shrine. When Elizabeth offered to preserve the monastery if the monks accepted the new religion, he refused. He defended the old faith in Parliament and went quietly on planting trees until the expulsion of July 1559. He died a prisoner at Wisbech Castle in 1585.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-pecham:
John Pecham was a Franciscan Archbishop of Canterbury known for fearless reform and unswerving principle. Born about 1240 at Patcham in Sussex, he was educated by the monks of Lewes and studied at Paris. He tutored a prince's nephew and entered the Friars Minor, teaching divinity at Oxford and becoming provincial before Rome made him lector of the sacred palace in 1276.

Elected to Canterbury in January 1279 over Edward I's candidate, he held councils at Reading and Lambeth against pluralities and for reverence toward the Eucharist. He visited every part of his province uprooting abuses and forced exempt royal chapels to submit to visitation. He intervened for Almeric de Montfort and warned Llewellyn in vain. He renewed at Oxford the condemnation of errors, some from Averroes and some from Aquinas, later commonly accepted, before his death in 1292.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-placid-a:
John Placid Adelham was a Benedictine monk who died in Newgate Prison as a victim of the Popish Plot. A Protestant minister born in Wiltshire, he became a Catholic and joined the Benedictines, professed at St. Edward's Monastery in Paris in 1652. He served as prior of St. Lawrence's at Dieulward from 1659 to 1661.

Sent to England, he was stationed at Somerset House from 1661 to 1675 and banished that year. He returned again, only to be caught in Titus Oates's fabricated Popish Plot. Tried and sentenced to death merely for being a priest on 17 January 1679, he was reprieved but detained in Newgate Prison. He died sometime between 1681 and 1685, one of the many quiet victims of that panic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kumbakonam:
Kumbakonam, the Jug's Corner in English, is a town of 60,000 in the fertile Tanjore plain, halfway by rail between Madras and Tuticorin. Of small weight to the British Raj, it ranks high for Hindus as home to one of the south's holiest shrines.

Legend tells how Siva, before the Deluge, had Brahma seal the spark of creation, the Vedas, and corn-seed in an earthen jug on ambrosia, set on Mount Meru. Flood waters bore it to the spot of today's sacred tank, the Maghamagham. Every twelve years a festival marks the event, when Jupiter meets the full moon in Magham. In 1909 it ran ten days from Kumbesshur temple, with some 800,000 pilgrims bathing for pardon and for their ancestors' salvation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mohammed-and-:
Mohammed, called the Praised One, founded Islam. He drew Arabia's rival tribes into one people with one faith, one law and one sanctuary. Born at Mecca around 570, he worked as a shepherd and caravan hand. He married the wealthy widow Khadeejah at twenty-five. At forty he claimed a call from the angel Gabriel, and his preaching began. Persecution drove him to Medina in 622, the year of the Hejira, from which the Muslim calendar counts.

Beyond the life story, the entry sets out the Koran's core teachings. It covers the traditions and scholars that interpret them, and the split between Sunni and Shia followers. It also maps the faith's reach near 1913. Roughly 170 million Muslims lived in Asia and 60 million in Africa. Smaller communities lived in Europe, America and Australia, and notes on its spread and its dealings with other religions close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-abra:
Nicholas Abram, Jesuit theologian, was born in 1589 at Xaronval in Lorraine and died on 7 September 1655. He taught rhetoric at Pont-a-Mousson, then undertook missionary work, and finally taught theology at Pont-a-Mousson for seventeen years. His principal works show a scholar of wide range.

They include a paraphrase of Nonnus of Panopolis on Saint John's Gospel with notes, published at Paris in 1623. Commentaries on Virgil's Bucolics and Georgics, with a diatribe on the four rivers and paradise's site, appeared at Pont-a-Mousson in 1633 to 1635. Pharus Veteris Testamenti, fifteen books of sacred questions with four books on truth and falsehood, appeared at Paris in 1648. The last counts as Father Abram's principal exegetical work, and Sommervogel lists his other writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-adam:
Nicholas Adam, linguist and writer, was born in Paris in 1716 and died in 1792. He won distinction through a peculiar grammar of his own, titled La vraie maniere d'apprendre une langue quelconque, vivante ou morte, par le moyen de la langue francaise. It comprised five grammars: French, Latin, Italian, German and English.

He published another book, Les quatre chapitres, on reason, self-love, love of neighbour and love of virtue, written in good and bad Latin and good and bad French. He left many translations of classic works, including Pope's Essay on Man, Johnson's Rasselas, Addison's Cato and Young's Night Thoughts. A favourite of Choiseul, who sent him as French ambassador to Venice, he reportedly knew all Europe's languages and gifted others with that knowledge. He long taught eloquence at Lisieux College.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nottingham:
Nottingham, one of the twelve English dioceses restored by Pius IX in 1850, covers Nottingham, Leicester, Derby, Lincoln, and Rutland. These counties formed the old Midland District, one of four vicariates into which England was split in 1685 at James II's request.

In 1850 the diocese counted only twenty-four permanent missions, many little more than villages, kept alive through penal times by Catholic gentry chaplaincies. Jesuits, Dominicans, Fathers of Charity, and Cistercians of Mount Saint Bernard carried those missions, and the entry traces their growth. Before 1840 the Midland District held fifteen counties, cut to eight vicariates in that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osbern-bokenh:
Osbern Bokenham was an English Augustinian friar and poet born in 1393 and probably dead by 1447. His birthplace likely lay near the Augustinian house at Bokenham, now Old Buckenham in Norfolk, though his German editor placed it at Bookham in Surrey. As a young man he spent five years in Italy, chiefly at Venice, and made pilgrimages to Rome and other centres of devotion.

Italy gave him a liberal schooling in a generation when Petrarch's memory was still fresh. He read Cicero and Ovid, rare feats for an English churchman of his day. His chief work, the Lyvys of Seyntys, retells the lives of twelve women saints, drawn mainly from the Golden Legend, with the tale of the 11,000 virgins. Written in Suffolk speech and ottava rima, it counts more as a landmark of English letters than as sound saint lore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-graha:
Patrick Graham was first Archbishop of Saint Andrews and Metropolitan of Scotland, dead in 1478, his birth date uncertain. Son of Mary, younger daughter of Robert III, by her third husband William Graham of Kincardine, he studied at Saint Andrews, where he served as dean of arts in 1457. He became Bishop of Brechin in 1463 and succeeded his half-brother, the famed Bishop Kennedy, at Saint Andrews in 1466.

Travelling to Rome for Paul II's confirmation, he stayed abroad till 1469 to dodge powerful nobles' enmity. There he won Saint Andrews' erection as archbishopric and metropolitan church, with Scotland's twelve other sees as suffragans, announced by Sixtus IV's bull of 27 August 1472. York, Trondheim, king, and Scottish bishops all resisted the change, made worse by Graham's naming as nuncio to raise crusade funds, and his fall followed swiftly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-franco:
Pierre François Xavier de Ram was a Belgian historian and rector of Louvain's Catholic University, born there on 2 September 1804. Of an ancient family from Zealand, he entered Mechlin Seminary and was ordained in 1827. While William I of the Netherlands campaigned against Belgian Catholic faith and traditions, the young priest joined the clergy's struggle, republishing eighteenth-century studies that refuted Joseph II and his disciple William.

He became keeper of Mechlin's diocesan records and professor at its seminary, and helped publish lives of the Netherlands' chief saints. Hagiography absorbed him for years. He edited Butler's Lives of the Saints from 1828 to 1835, and from 1828 to 1858 issued the four-volume Synodicon Belgicum, unpublished documents on Netherlands church history since Philip II. After the 1830 revolution he served Louvain's university, treating its history in monographs from Brussels' National Archives. His complete works, listed in 1880, number 205 volumes. He died at Louvain in 1865.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-tua:
Tuam, Irish Tuaim da Ghualann, Mound of the Two Shoulders, was founded by Jarlath and already in his lifetime, ending about 540, ranked as a famed school of piety and learning. By the eleventh century it matched Clonmacnoise as a hub of Celtic art. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a school born of friendship.

Jarlath trained under Benignus, Patrick's successor and helper, and founded his first monastery at Cluainfois, now Cloonfush, two miles west of Tuam near Benignus's Kilbannon. There Benignus, Jarlath, and Caillin, another disciple, often met to debate theology and Scripture. Scholars came from all Ireland, among them Brendan the navigator from Kerry and Colman son of Lenin from Cloyne, drawn by the retreat's growing fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simeon-of-dur:
Simeon of Durham, also spelled Symeon, was a chronicler who died on 14 October between 1130 and 1138. As a youth he entered the Benedictine monastery at Jarrow, moved to Durham in 1074, and was professed in 1085 or 1086, later becoming precentor. His chief work, the History of the Church of Durham, written between 1104 and 1108, carries the bishopric's history to 1096.

He also wrote a History of the Kings of the English and Danes, running from 732 to 1129. Its first part, to 957, rests on a northern annalist who drew heavily on Asser. The next part, to 1119, follows Florence of Worcester. The remainder is Simeon's own composition. His authorship, challenged by Bale and Selden, was vindicated by Rudd in 1732. Minor works include a letter on the archbishops of York, written about 1130, and letters now lost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-langham:
Simon Langham, cardinal, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Chancellor of England, was born at Langham in Rutland and died at Avignon on 22 July 1376. Nothing is known of his early life. By 1346 he was a Benedictine monk of Westminster Abbey. In April 1349 he became prior, and in May, abbot. As abbot he ruled well and completed the cloisters. He became treasurer of England in 1360 and Bishop of Ely in 1362.

He refused election as Bishop of London, preferring Ely. On 19 February 1363 he received the great seal as chancellor, and he was the first to open Parliament in English. Appointed Archbishop of Canterbury in July 1366, he watched against false doctrine and condemned Oxford propositions. He removed a namesake Wycliffe from Canterbury Hall and censured the priest John Ball. Made cardinal in 1368 without royal leave, he offended Edward III, lost the Canterbury revenues, and resigned the see in November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-thomas-me:
Thomas Metham, knight and confessor of the faith, died in York Castle in 1573. Eldest son of Thomas Metham of Metham, Yorkshire, he married twice, first Dorothy, daughter of Lord Darcy and Meinill, then Edith, daughter of Nicholas Palmes of Naburn. On 2 October 1553, the day after Queen Mary's coronation, he received a knighthood of the carpet. 

By August 1565 he and his second wife were jailed for contempt of royal ordinances on divine service and sacraments. A correspondent wrote to Cecil in February 1570 calling him a most willful papist, utterly refusing service, Communion, or any books but Rome-approved ones. He maintained two sons at Louvain, and growing daily wealthier and more willful after four years in ward. Revered by papists as a pillar of their faith, he was moved to York Castle, where he remained and died, steadfast to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-thomas-tr:
Thomas Tresham, Knight Bachelor by 1524 and Grand Prior of England in the Hospitaller Order of Saint John of Jerusalem from 1557. Of unknown birth date, he died on 8 March 1559. He served as sheriff of Northamptonshire in 1524, 1539, 1545, and 1555, and sat for the county in 1541 and twice in 1554.

He served constantly on commissions of the peace, gaol delivery, oyer and terminer, and sewers. He acted as special commissioner to search for grain in 1527, to inquire into Wolsey's possessions in 1530, and into the Lincolnshire rebellion in 1537. In 1539 he helped receive Anne of Cleves at Calais. In 1540 he gained license to enclose the Lyveden estate, where his grandson's New Bield still stands. In 1544 he supplied men for France, and in 1546 he assessed the Contribution Commission. Under Mary he regained Hospitaller lands worth one thousand four hundred thirty-six pounds a year, sat in the Lords in January 1558, and was buried at Rushton with great pomp.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-emmeram:
Emmeram, missionary bishop to Bavaria, carried the faith from Poitiers down the Danube and died for it on the road. Born at Poitiers in the early seventh century to a noble Aquitanian family, he was ordained priest and may briefly have held the see of Poitiers. Hearing Bavaria was still pagan, he crossed the Black Forest, descended the Danube, and reached Ratisbon under Duke Theodo. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 gives his martyrdom at Ascheim late in the century.

For three years he preached and converted across Bavaria, winning renown for holiness. Setting out for Rome to visit the tombs of Peter and Paul, he was attacked after five days at Kleinhelfendorf, south of Munich. The entry leaves his Poitiers tenure uncertain, but his Bavarian mission and violent end stand at its centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gilbert-of:
Gilbert of Sempringham, founder of the Gilbertines, built England's only native monastic order from a Lincolnshire fen parish. Born between 1083 and 1089 to Jocelin, a wealthy Norman knight, and an English mother of humble rank, he was ill-favoured and deformed, so no knightly career awaited him. Sent to study in France, he taught there, then returned to livings at Sempringham and Tirington in his father's gift. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Sempringham to 1189.

At Bishop Robert Bloet's court he became a household clerk, and Alexander, Robert's successor, ordained him deacon and priest much against his will. Sempringham's revenues kept him at court, while Tirington's went elsewhere. In old age he refused an oath over Becket, lest it paint him the archbishop's enemy, though he had sent no help. The entry closes on a founder of vast age and stubborn conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william:
William Fitzherbert, archbishop of York, won his see, lost it, and won it again amid charges of simony. Tradition makes him nephew of King Stephen, whose sister Emma supposedly married Herbert of Winchester, treasurer to Henry I. A priest by about 1130, he was canon and treasurer of York, and in 1142 was elected archbishop at the king's instance over Henry Murdac, a Cistercian.

The election's validity was disputed for alleged simony and royal pressure, and Theobald refused consecration pending appeal to Rome. Bernard pressed Murdac's cause, but in 1143 the pope ruled William should be consecrated if he cleared himself of bribery and the chapter showed no undue royal pressure. He did, and the legate consecrated him at Winchester on 26 September 1143. Deposed in 1147, he was restored in 1153 and died weeks later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wulfram:
Wulfram, bishop of Sens and missionary to the Frisians, tried to convert King Radbod and failed. Born at Milly near Fontainebleau, probably under Clovis II, who reigned from 638 to 656, he was son of Fulbert, high in Dagobert I's and Clovis II's esteem. Well educated and ordained priest, he meant to live secluded but was called to Theodoric III's court.

From there he rose to the see of Sens in 684, 690, or 692, and attended a bishops' assembly at Valenciennes in 693. Two years later he resigned and retired to Fontanelle abbey. During Boniface's second journey to Rome he is said to have preached in Frisia, labouring to convert Radbod without success before returning to Fontanelle. His relics reached Notre Dame at Abbeville in 1058, and his feast falls on 20 March.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-rowsh:
This Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows Stephen Rowsham, an Oxfordshire priest who died for his faith in Elizabethan England. Rowsham entered Oriel College, Oxford, in 1572, served as a minister in the Church of England, then changed allegiance to Rome. He trained at Reims in France, received priestly ordination there in 1581, and came back to England on mission work the next year.

Arrest followed almost at once after his landing, and he spent more than three years locked up, much of it in a cramped Tower cell called the Little Ease. After a spell in the Marshalsea prison he was sent into exile in 1585, yet returned within months to work in the west of England. Seized at a house in Gloucester, he faced trial there and was put to death in March 1587. A list of early sources closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-books-of-:
Writings gathered around Adam, the first parent, are catalogued in this compact entry. Chief among them stands the Book of Adam, or Contradiction of Adam and Eve, a romance woven from Oriental fables. Dillmann rendered it from Ethiopic into German in 1853, and Malan into English in 1882.

Kindred texts follow. The Penitence of Adam comes from Syrian fragments translated by Renan, and a Latin Penitence was published by Meyer in 1879. The Books of the Daughters of Adam appear in Pope Gelasius's catalogue of 495, and the Testament of Our First Parents is cited by Anastasius the Sinaite. Together they show how early Christians imagined Adam's life after Eden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bosom-of-:
A phrase found only in Luke chapter 16, verses 22 and 23, is unpacked here: the Bosom of Abraham. It appears in the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus, whose imagery draws on popular pictures of the unseen world current in Christ's day. Jewish thought then gathered the dead in Sheol, or Hades, a general waiting place divided by deed.

Righteous souls occupied a compartment of bliss and safety, separated by wall or chasm from the wicked, whose portion was torment in Gehenna. That blessed abode bore several names, among them Paradise and the Bosom of Abraham. The entry traces the phrase through Scripture, Fathers, and liturgy, and explains its place in later teaching on the afterlife.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-messin:
Thomas Messingham, an Irish hagiologist of the Diocese of Meath, devoted his life to the saints of Ireland and to the Irish College at Paris. By 1615 he was on the college staff in Paris, gathering material on Irish saints. In 1620 he published offices of Patrick, Brigid, Columba and other Irish saints.

In 1621 he succeeded his friend Thomas Dease as rector of the Irish College, Paris, after Dease became Bishop of Meath. Honoured by the Holy See as prothonotary apostolic, Messingham organized the college course to send capable missionaries home. He won its affiliation to the University of Paris, and in 1624 published his Florilegium Insulae Sanctorum, with a treatise on St. Patrick's Purgatory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-walsin:
Thomas Walsingham, a Benedictine historian who died about 1422, chronicled late medieval England from St. Albans Abbey. Probably a native of Walsingham, Norfolk, he was educated at St. Albans, became a monk there, and served as precentor in charge of the scriptorium. In 1394 he became superior of the dependent priory of Wymondham, returning to St. Albans in 1409.

Six chronicles are assigned to him, though authorship is not always certain. The Chronicon Angliae covers 1328 to 1388 and criticizes John of Gaunt rather sharply, while the Gesta Abbatum records the abbots of St. Albans between 1390 and 1394, drawing heavily on Matthew Paris. A later St. Albans chronicle, running from 1272 to 1393, softens the criticism of Gaunt, perhaps because the monks feared Henry IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-wingha:
Thomas Wingham, a composer born in London in 1846, shaped the musical life of the Brompton Oratory. He studied at Wylde's London Academy and then at the Royal Academy of Music, where Sterndale Bennett taught him theory and Harold Thomas taught him piano. He later became professor of piano at the Royal Academy himself.

At about the same time he became choirmaster at the Brompton Oratory, and the artistic quality of its performances soon proved his musicianship. He prepared the way for the liturgical music that followed there. His works include four symphonies, six overtures, two masses and a Te Deum, most of which stayed in manuscript though often performed in his lifetime. He died in London in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tuam:
The Archdiocese of Tuam, metropolitan see of Connacht, stretching roughly from the Shannon westward to the sea. Territorially the largest diocese in Ireland, it holds about one-fourteenth of the country, with a Catholic population of 193,768 at the 1901 census against only 4,194 non-Catholics.

A chain of lakes, Corrib, Mask and Carra, divides arable eastern plains from a rugged, heathy west, where steep hills and deep, fish-filled lakes draw anglers from across the United Kingdom. The entry also traces the archbishops' long dispute with Armagh over Patrician churches, settled at Rome after the Synod of Kells in 1152.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unam-sanctam:
Unam Sanctam is the bull on papal supremacy issued by Boniface VIII on 18 November 1302, during his quarrel with Philip the Fair of France. Its name comes from its opening words, meaning the one holy church. The bull was proclaimed in connection with the Roman council of October 1302, where it had probably been discussed. Boniface himself may have revised the text, and Aegidius Colonna, Archbishop of Bourges, who defied the royal ban to attend, seems to have shaped it.

The original is lost, and the oldest text survives in Boniface's Vatican registers. The bull was later taken into the body of canon law. Its central claim is that the spiritual power stands above the temporal, and that submission to the Roman pontiff is necessary for salvation. The entry sets out the bull's wording, its sources, and the storm it raised in France, where royal lawyers answered it with pamphlets and protests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-ingr:
John Ingram was an English martyr born at Stoke Edith in Herefordshire in 1565, executed at Newcastle-on-Tyne on 26 July 1594. Probably the son of Anthony Ingram of Wolford by Dorothy Hungerford, he studied first in Worcestershire. He then studied at the English College, Reims, at the Jesuit College of Pont-à-Mousson, and at the English College, Rome. Ordained at Rome in 1589, he set out for Scotland early in 1592.

There he kept company with Lords Huntly, Angus, and Erroll, the Abbot of Dumfries, and Sir Walter Lindsay of Balgavies. Captured on the Tyne on 25 November 1593, he was jailed in turn at Berwick, Durham, York, and the Tower of London. There he bore the severest tortures with great constancy and wrote twenty Latin epigrams that survive. Sent north again, he was tried and executed at Newcastle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-tho:
Thomas Belchiam was a Franciscan friar who died in prison in August 1537 for opposing Henry VIII. A member of the Observant Franciscans, the stricter branch of the order, he boldly opposed the king's divorces and denounced him as a heretic.

Belchiam wrote a book for his brethren, opening with the text about those who wear soft clothing living in kings' houses, rebuking bishops too afraid to tell the king the truth. The book is lost, but one copy reached Henry, who was said to have wept reading it before repenting of that weakness. Belchiam and some thirty Observants were thrown into prison, where they perished of hunger.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Kottayam is a vicariate on India's Malabar Coast belonging to the ancient Church of Malabar. Traditionally founded by St Thomas and governed by Syro-Chaldean bishops until the Portuguese replaced them with Latin bishops in 1600. Until 1887 its Syrian Catholics lived under the Latin bishops of Verapoly, Cranganore, and Goa.

Leo XIII's brief of 1887 separated the Syrian-rite churches into the vicariates of Trichur and Kottayam, independent of Verapoly. A new division in 1896 suppressed Kottayam among Trichur, Ernakulam, and Changanacherry. Pius X restored it in 1911 for the Suddhists, Syro-Malabar Christians descended from fourth-century Syrian immigrants, covering all their churches and chapels in Ernakulam and Changanacherry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vizagapatam:
Vizagapatam is a diocese in eastern India, suffragan to Madras, bounded by the Mahanadi River, the Godavari, Nagpur diocese, and the Bay of Bengal. Though within the Portuguese diocese of Mylapore from 1606 and the Madras vicariate from 1834, almost no missionary work was done there until it became a vicariate in 1845.

The first fathers found one old Theatine priest, last survivor of the Golconda mission. Only scattered Catholics, mostly European troops or camp followers, about four thousand in 1850, when the vicariate still included all the Nagpur districts. Those districts were made a diocese in 1887, when Vizagapatam also became a diocese, both suffragan to Madras. Its prelates to 1910 ran from Vicar Apostolic Theophilus Sebastian Neyret, 1849 to 1862, through John M. Tissot, first bishop in 1887, to John Mary Clerc, installed in 1891.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william:
William, Abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, was a Cluniac reformer of the eleventh century. Born on Giuglio island in Lake Orta near Novara in 962, he died at Fécamp on 1 January 1031. Brought as an oblate at seven to Locedia, he moved to Cluny in 987. A year later Majolus sent him to reform Saint-Saturnin near Avignon, and on his return in 990 he became Abbot of Saint-Bénigne and took priesthood that June.

From Dijon, William spread Cluny's strict discipline through monasteries in Normandy, Burgundy, and Lorraine. Langres set him over every house in its diocese, and he ruled more than forty monasteries and twelve hundred monks. He founded schools for monks, candidates, and layfolk, and at Saint-Bénigne raised a Romanesque church between 1001 and 1018, then France's most beautiful. Though never formally canonized, he is honoured as a saint with a feast on 1 January.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-oc:
William of Ockham was a fourteenth-century Franciscan thinker whose razor still shapes how we argue. Born near Ockham in Surrey about 1280, he died at Munich about 1349. Said to have studied at Merton College, Oxford, under Duns Scotus, he joined the Franciscans young and taught at Paris about 1320. He wrote on Aristotle's physics and on logic before quitting his chair in 1323 for church politics.

Ockham backed the imperial side against the papacy, fled Avignon's summons in 1328, and joined Louis of Bavaria. He offered, in his famous boast, to defend the king with his pen if the king defended him with the sword. His law of parsimony, that beings need not multiply needlessly, drove a push to simplify thought and doubt. He denied mental species, essence-existence splits, and reason's proof of God or the soul, leaving those truths to revelation. He made right and wrong rest on God's will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-sh:
William of Shoreham was an English religious poet of the Anglo-Norman age and possibly the maker of the earliest full English Psalter. Born at Shoreham near Sevenoaks in Kent in the later twelfth century, he died on an unknown date. In 1313 he became vicar of Chart Sutton in Kent, a living of Leeds Priory, which suggests he was an Austin canon there. His name in colophons to several poems secures his authorship of the verse.

His poems and the Psalter share one manuscript and one hand in the British Museum, Additional Manuscripts 17376, and Thomas Wright edited the poems for the Percy Society in 1849. Doubt hangs over the Psalter alone: it speaks Mercian dialect, not Kentish, so some scholars deny it to him. If his, it stands as the earliest complete English rendering of the Psalms, a milestone for vernacular Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-wy:
William of Wykeham was Bishop of Winchester, Chancellor of England, and founder of Winchester College and New College, Oxford. Born at Wickham in Hampshire between July and September 1324, he died on 27 September 1404. Schooled at Winchester, he served the castle constable, caught Bishop Edington's eye and then Edward III's, entering royal service about twenty-three as architect and surveyor, overseeing Windsor Castle's rebuilding.

Rewarded, in the bad custom of the age, with church livings before he held even minor orders, he took those in December 1361 and priesthood the next year. As keeper of the privy seal from 1364, Froissart said he reigned in England. Elected Bishop of Winchester in October 1366 and chancellor a month before his 1367 consecration, he lost the seal in 1372 amid French war reverses. He faced impeachment by John of Gaunt in 1376 with his revenues seized, yet won full pardon under Richard II. He raised his great colleges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-warha:
William Warham was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1503 and Lord Chancellor under Henry VII and Henry VIII. Born at Church Oakley about 1450, he died at Hackington near Canterbury in 1532. Schooled at Winchester and New College, Oxford, where he became a fellow in 1475 and a doctor of laws, he practised in London's church courts, then led Oxford's civil law school. Embassies abroad won him church posts and, in 1494, the mastership of the rolls.

Elected Bishop of London in October 1501 and consecrated in September 1502, Warham gave up the rolls for the Great Seal. Julius II named him Canterbury archbishop in November 1503, and the king made him chancellor in January 1504. He crowned Henry VIII and Katherine in 1509 and served as Oxford's chancellor from 1506. Wolsey's rise pushed him to second place; he quit the chancellorship before Christmas 1515 and watched the cardinal overrule him as legate until his health failed amid the divorce crisis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-williram:
Williram was an eleventh-century Bible scholar whose three-column Song of Songs paraphrase charmed medieval Germany. Born in Franconia near Worms, he died at Ebersberg in Bavaria in 1085. Pupil of the famed Lanfranc, he may have studied at Paris, gave up the Bamberg cathedral school post, and retired to Fulda monastery. Henry III then called him to rule the Benedictine abbey at Ebersberg, which he governed with success for thirty-seven years until his death.

Williram's fame rests on his translation and paraphrase of the Canticle of Canticles. Its preface laments that Germany prizes grammar and logic above Scripture and praises Lanfranc for drawing German scholars to Bible study in France. Each page sets three columns side by side: a Latin paraphrase in Leonine hexameters, the Vulgate text, and a German prose exposition, reading the whole song allegorically as Christ and the Church. Many surviving manuscripts attest its welcome.
christianity-and-islam:
C. H. Becker, professor of Oriental history at Hamburg's Colonial Institute, wrote a comparison translated by Rev. H. J. Chaytor and published in 1909. Becker begins by separating motives. A missionary, a churchman hunting proof, and a historian will each compare the two faiths differently. His own aim is historical connection, not verdict.

Three parts follow the traffic both ways. First, Christianity's influence on Muhammad and on Islam's rise. Second, the likeness of Christian and Muslim thought in the middle ages — asceticism, ritual, mysticism, saints, and scholastic dogma. Muslim warnings against fine building are traced to inherited Christian polemic. Third, Islam's influence back upon Christianity, including philosophy. A bibliography closes a compact, scholarly survey.
cicero-de-legibus-barham:
Cicero's On the Laws, begun around 52 BC, is the sequel to his On the Republic. Francis Barham's English translation of 1841 and 1842 is the text here, from the Online Library of Liberty. Cicero talks with his brother Quintus and his friend Atticus as they walk his home grounds.

He argues that true law is right reason shared with the gods, older than any written code. From that root he frames model laws for religion and for the officers of the state. The work survives in part, breaking off before its plan was done. It is the founding text of natural law thought, the idea that unjust commands are not true laws.
cowper-works-cunningham:
Gathered in one volume in 1854, The Works of William Cowper joins a life of the poet with his letters and his poems. Cowper, born in 1731 and dead by 1800, lived much of his writing life in quiet country retirement. A portrait drawn from life in 1782 faces the title page of this edition.

Readers get The Task, the hymns, and translations beside the letters that made him famous in his own day. Friends such as Lady Hesketh saved those letters for their warmth and humor. Together the parts form a full portrait of a gentle, often sad man whose plain words reshaped English poetry.
de-amicitia-scipio-s-dream:
Cicero's De Amicitia, with Scipio's Dream, translated by Andrew P. Peabody, presents the Roman statesman's treatise on friendship. Peabody's synopsis follows Laelius, famed for wisdom, as friends ask how he bore the death of Scipio, and what grounds consoled him.

Laelius expresses faith in immortality and a desire that the friendship of Scipio and himself be remembered forever. Later sections define true friendship as possible only among good men, weigh utility against nature as its foundation, and set limits to what friends may ask of each other. Readers of classical philosophy will find Cicero's essay humane, practical and enduringly quotable.
